# Prune and Rename

After this page you can tell a stale remote-tracking branch from a still-live server branch, prune the stale names with `git fetch --prune`, and rename a remote when "origin" is no longer the right label.

## Thesis

`git fetch` updates the remote-tracking refs under `refs/remotes/<remote>/` to match the server. By default it **adds and updates** those refs; it does **not** delete a local remote-tracking branch just because the server deleted the branch. The leftover name keeps looking like a real remote branch in `git branch -r` until you prune.

Renaming a remote (`git remote rename`) rewrites the remote's URL slots, the `refs/remotes/` namespace, and the upstream configuration on branches that pointed at it. Prune and rename are how you keep that map honest as remotes come and go.

Verified with **git 2.47.3** against two local bare repositories (no network).

## Mental model

```text
  server (origin)                 your clone
  refs/heads/main        <--fetch-->  refs/remotes/origin/main
  refs/heads/stale  (deleted)         refs/remotes/origin/stale  <- leftover
                                      refs/heads/stale           <- local branch, untouched by prune
```

`git fetch --prune origin` deletes `origin/stale` once the server no longer has `stale`. It does not delete your local branch `stale`. After a rename, a local branch whose upstream vanished is reported as `[upstream/stale: gone]`.

## Lab

Two bare repos stand in for "upstream" and a "fork". The work clone starts with `origin` pointing at upstream.

```text
[main (root-commit) 312d103] initial
To /tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/upstream.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
Switched to a new branch 'stale'
[stale 0049373] stale work
To /tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/upstream.git
 * [new branch]      stale -> stale
branch 'stale' set up to track 'origin/stale'.
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
Deleted branch stale (was 0049373).
===== remote heads after server deleted stale =====
312d103e17b8485af0b36f4fffb4d637f7a03605	refs/heads/main
===== local remote-tracking before fetch =====
  origin/main
  origin/stale
===== fetch without prune =====
tracking after fetch (no prune):
  origin/main
  origin/stale
===== fetch --prune =====
From /tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/upstream
 - [deleted]         (none)     -> origin/stale
tracking after prune:
  origin/main
===== rename remote origin -> upstream =====
upstream	/tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/upstream.git (fetch)
upstream	/tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/upstream.git (push)
* main  312d103 [upstream/main] initial
  stale 0049373 [upstream/stale: gone] stale work
To /tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/fork.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
===== remotes after adding fork as origin =====
origin	/tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/fork.git (fetch)
origin	/tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/fork.git (push)
upstream	/tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/upstream.git (fetch)
upstream	/tmp/r1112-labs/vcs/upstream.git (push)
```

The line `Deleted branch stale (was 0049373).` is the **server** deletion (`git --git-dir=upstream.git branch -D stale`). The work clone still has a local `stale` branch afterwards; prune only removed `origin/stale`. After `git remote rename origin upstream`, that local branch is still there, now tracking a missing `upstream/stale` (`gone`). Adding a new remote named `origin` that points at the fork is then safe: the old server became `upstream`.

A plain `git fetch origin` after the server delete printed nothing about `stale` and left `origin/stale` in place. Only `--prune` advertised the deletion.

You can make prune the default for a remote with `git config fetch.prune true` or `git config remote.origin.prune true`. This lab used the explicit flag.

## Pitfalls

1. Treating `git branch -r` as a live server inventory — without prune it includes ghosts.
2. Expecting `git fetch --prune` to delete your **local** branch of the same name. It will not. Delete that yourself when you are done (`git branch -d stale`), and only after you have decided the work is disposable.
3. Renaming `origin` in a script that later assumes the name `origin` still points at the same host.
4. Pruning automatically in a clone that uses unusual refspecs you have not reviewed — check `remote.<name>.fetch` first.

## Worked scenarios

### Scenario A — a teammate deleted the branch on the server

`git fetch` still shows `origin/topic`. Run `git fetch --prune` and look for `- [deleted] (none) -> origin/topic`. If you still have a local `topic`, `git branch -vv` will eventually show `[origin/topic: gone]` once the tracking name is gone or after a rename as in the lab.

### Scenario B — you forked, and "origin" should mean your fork

Rename the upstream remote first (`git remote rename origin upstream`), then `git remote add origin <fork-url>` and push, as the lab did. Fetch and push defaults then go to the fork; `upstream` remains available for `git fetch upstream`.

### Scenario C — dry-run before pruning

`git remote prune origin --dry-run` (not run in this lab) lists what would be deleted without changing refs. Use it when you are unsure why a name is disappearing.

## Summary

- `git fetch` does not delete stale remote-tracking branches unless you prune.
- `git fetch --prune <remote>` drops tracking refs the server no longer has; local branches stay.
- `git remote rename` rewrites URLs, remote-tracking names, and upstream configuration.
- `[remote/branch: gone]` means this local branch still exists but its configured upstream ref does not.
